`docs/deployment.md`:

```md
# Deploying a node (production checklist)

Step-by-step order for go-live and every release: [release-checklist.md](release-checklist.md).

## Network

- Postgres and Redis on a private network only, with authentication (`DATABASE_URL`
  with a strong password and `sslmode=require`; Redis `requirepass`/ACL via `redis://:password@host`, TLS via `rediss://` (built in), or a private
  link). The node never exposes them.
- Public ports: `server.http_addr` (TCP, control plane + WS tunnel), `transport.quic_addr`
  (UDP), `transport.webtransport_addr` (UDP). Everything else closed.
- Terminate TLS for the HTTP port at a reverse proxy or load balancer (the node speaks plain
  HTTP there; `deploy/Caddyfile.example` is a working two-node Caddy config with health-checked
  round robin that drops draining nodes) and put the proxy's address range into `server.trusted_proxies` so per-IP limits
  see real client addresses via `X-Forwarded-For`. QUIC/WebTransport use the node's own
  certificate (`transport.cert_pem`/`key_pem`); browsers need a publicly trusted one.
- Keep `/metrics` off the public interface or set `server.metrics_token`.

## Configuration

`server.heartbeat_secs` (default 30) is stored with the node's row; peers declare a node dead after it
misses three of *its own* heartbeats, so nodes with different intervals can share a fleet (a 2 s dev node
next to a 30 s one). Unknown `NET__<SECTION>__…` variables are reported with a startup warning.

`server.public_host` is also what the other nodes use to reach this one for operator calls
(`GET /v1/operator/nodes/:id/stats`, drains): it must resolve and route *inside* the cluster, not only from
the internet. The compose file defaults to the service names (`node-a`, `node-b`), which is right for a
single-host stack; across hosts set `NODE_A_PUBLIC_HOST`/`NODE_B_PUBLIC_HOST` in `.env` to real hostnames.

```toml
[server]
environment = "production"      # enables the secret checks below
region = "eu-central"
public_host = "node-1.eu.example.com"
trusted_proxies = ["10.0.0.0/8"]
metrics_token = "<random>"

[auth]
grant_secret = "<32+ random bytes>"   # shared by all nodes of a deployment
admin_token = "<random>"              # or empty to disable operator endpoints

[transport]
cert_pem = "..."                      # or a path via NET__TRANSPORT__CERT_PEM
key_pem = "..."
```

Everything can also come from the environment (`NET__AUTH__GRANT_SECRET=...`). Secrets must
not be baked into images or committed; use your orchestrator's secret store.

## Process

- Run as an unprivileged user; raise `nofile` (one fd per connection, ≥ 65536).
- Send `SIGTERM` to stop. The node marks itself draining (new joins refused, `/healthz` 503),
  checkpoints every room to Redis and marks them `orphaned`; the next node a player reaches
  adopts the room. Give it ≥ 10 s before `SIGKILL`. Rolling deploys with ≥ 2 nodes per region
  therefore do not end matches.
- Readiness probe: `GET /healthz` (200 = serving, 503 = draining). Liveness: TCP on the HTTP
  port.

## Limits worth tuning

`limits.*` in the config are node-wide ceilings; per-project quotas are set with the operator
API. Defaults: 64 sessions per IP, 50 HTTP rps per IP, 60 WS connects/min per IP, 20 auth
failures/min per IP, 20 writes/s per API key, 2000 events/s per room, 60 per player.

## Upgrades

Nodes of one deployment should run the same minor version; the room checkpoint format is
versioned in JSON and tolerates added fields.

Rolling upgrade, one node at a time (verified on the reference compose: `stop` returned in
0.4 s, the node logged `shutdown: rooms handed off rooms=1`, the room was listed from the other
node immediately and the first node served `/healthz` 200 again 6 s after `start`):

```sh
docker compose pull            # or build the new image
docker compose up -d --no-deps node-a   # SIGTERM → drain → rooms orphaned in Redis → exit 0
curl -fs http://node-a:8090/healthz     # wait for 200
docker compose up -d --no-deps node-b
```

Players of the drained node get `left{reason:"rehost"}` and rejoin by room name on any node;
the room's state comes from the checkpoint. Keep ≥ 2 nodes per region or a deploy ends matches.

## Migrations

The node applies `migrations/` (sqlx, forward-only, additive) on every start under Postgres'
migration lock, so two nodes starting together do not race. For a controlled rollout run the
new image once with `--migrate-only` (connects, migrates, exits 0 — no Redis needed) before
replacing nodes; the old version keeps running against the migrated schema until it is swapped.
There is no down migration: restore from backup to roll a schema change back.

All row queries name their columns (no `SELECT *`), so a migration that adds a column does not break
the previous release's prepared statements (`cached plan must not change result type`). The one
exception is upgrading across `0012` from an older build: restart those nodes right after migrating.

## Secrets and rotation

| Secret | Where | Rotation |
|---|---|---|
| `auth.grant_secret` | all nodes of a deployment + your backend never sees it (it calls `/v1/grants`) | set the old value as `auth.grant_secret_previous`, new value as `grant_secret`, rolling-restart; grants signed with either verify until you drop `_previous` after ≥ `grant_ttl_secs` |
| `auth.admin_token` | nodes, operators | change and rolling-restart; operator sessions re-authenticate |
| API keys | your backend | `POST /v1/operator/projects/:id/keys` with `expires_in_secs`, switch the backend, revoke the old key — no restart |
| `server.metrics_token` | nodes, Prometheus | change both, rolling-restart |
| Postgres / Redis passwords | nodes, `.env` | change on the server, update `NET__DATABASE__URL` / `NET__REDIS__URL`, rolling-restart |
| Webhook secrets | per webhook | `POST /v1/webhooks/:id/rotate {grace_secs}` — new secret shown once, deliveries carry `X-Aurix-Signature-Previous` until the grace ends (default 24 h) |

Transport tickets (QUIC/WebTransport) are also keyed from `grant_secret` but are issued and
verified by the same node within seconds, so rotation needs no grace period for them.

## Backups

Postgres holds everything durable (projects, keys, room history, usage, audit, modules);
Redis holds live state (room index, checkpoints of orphaned rooms, rate-limit windows) and is
`appendonly yes` in the reference compose, so a Redis restart alone loses nothing.
`scripts/backup.sh [out-dir]` takes a consistent `pg_dump` (single transaction, plain SQL,
gzip) plus a point-in-time Redis RDB (`BGSAVE`, waits for `LASTSAVE` to move) and writes a
manifest with sizes and SHA-256; restore steps are in the script header. Run it from cron on
the compose host (`COMPOSE="docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file .env"`)
and ship the directory off-host; the dump contains API-key hashes and webhook secrets, so
treat it like the database itself.

## Docker

`Dockerfile` builds a release node image on `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot` (glibc + CA roots,
no shell/package manager; the previous bookworm-slim base carried ~46 unfixed HIGH CVEs in packages the node
never used), runs as uid 65532, `HEALTHCHECK` is the binary itself (`aurix-net-server --healthcheck` probes
its own `/healthz`), `STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM`
(the node drains and hands rooms off; give it `stop_grace_period: 30s`), container healthcheck on
`/healthz` (503 while draining, so orchestrators stop routing to it). Ports: 8090/tcp (HTTP/WS),
7000/udp (QUIC), 7443/udp (WebTransport). Configure with `NET__SECTION__KEY` env vars
(`NET__AUTH__GRANT_SECRET`, `NET__AUTH__ADMIN_TOKEN`, `NET__DATABASE__URL`, `NET__REDIS__URL`,
`NET__SERVER__PUBLIC_HOST`, ...) or mount a TOML and pass `--config /etc/aurix-net/net.toml` (needed
for list values such as `trusted_proxies` / `allowed_origins`). `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` is a
two-node reference layout. The image sets `NET__SERVER__HTTP_ADDR=0.0.0.0:8090` (the bare binary
defaults to 127.0.0.1 for dev runs; inside a container that leaves the published port dead while the
in-container healthcheck still passes — found when bringing the reference compose up). The console's
`NET_API_URL` should point at your load balancer / VIP, not one node, or the console returns 502
while that node is being upgraded.
CI publishes a CycloneDX SBOM of the node binary (`sbom` artifact, `cargo cyclonedx`) and runs `cargo audit` /
`cargo deny`; scan the built image with Trivy/Grype before promoting it (`trivy image aurix-net:<tag>`).

Postgres over TLS: `database.url = "postgres://user:pw@host/aurix_net?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/aurix-net/pg-ca.pem"`
(`require` for a public CA; the node fails at start on a certificate it cannot verify, it never falls back
to plaintext).

Redis over TLS: `redis.url = "rediss://:password@host:6390/"`; for a private CA set `redis.ca_cert` to the
PEM path (`NET__REDIS__CA_CERT=/etc/aurix-net/redis-ca.pem`), otherwise WebPKI roots are used.

## Monitoring

`/metrics` is Prometheus text (`server.metrics_token` as bearer; keep the port off the public
interface). `deploy/monitoring/` ships a ready stack:

- `prometheus.yml` — scrape config with the token from a file and a `node` label per target;
- `alerts.yml` — rules: node down, sync tick p99 > 10 ms, tick overruns, lockstep desync, > 2 % lost
  sync deltas, credential guessing being rate limited, Redis checkpoint write errors, rooms near
  `max_rooms_per_node`;
- `grafana/` — provisioned datasource and the **Aurix Net — fleet** dashboard (rooms/players per
  node, datagrams and bytes, tick p50/p99, overruns, events by channel, errors by code, sync health,
  desyncs/adopted rooms).

`docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml --profile monitoring up -d` starts Prometheus and
Grafana (`:3000`, password `GRAFANA_PASSWORD`) next to the nodes. For operator-facing alerts (node
stale, project at a usage cap, failing webhooks) the node itself can POST to a webhook — see
[webhooks.md](webhooks.md#operator-alerts-fleet-level); the Prometheus rules cover what only the
process knows (tick time, lost deltas, Redis writes).

## Console

`dashboard/` builds to a Caddy image (`aurix-net-console`, non-root, ~120 MB) that serves the
static console and reverse-proxies `/v1/*` and `/healthz` to one node (`NET_API_URL`, default
`http://net:8090`). It stores nothing: operator tokens and project API keys live in the
operator's browser (local storage) and are revalidated against `/v1/me` on every load.

- Put the console behind the same TLS terminator as the nodes; never expose it on plain HTTP
  outside a private network — the bearer token travels in every request.
- `server.allowed_origins` on the nodes does not need the console origin: the proxy keeps
  everything same-origin.
- The console only needs the node's HTTP port; QUIC/WebTransport ports are for game clients.
- Reference service: `console` in `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`. Local dev:
  `cd dashboard && npm ci && NET_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090 npm run dev`.
- Cross-node room detail: a node that does not host the room asks the hosting node over
  `GET /v1/internal/rooms/:id/players` with the fleet-wide `auth.admin_token`, so all nodes must
  share the same admin token and reach each other's `http_url`.

```

`docs/modes.md`:

```md
# Room modes

One server, one client, one wire format. A room is created in one of three modes; the mode
decides who runs the game simulation and what travels on the data path.

| | `relay` | `sync` | `lockstep` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simulation runs on | clients (your code) | server (authoritative) | every client (deterministic) |
| Client sends | events | inputs | inputs |
| Client receives | events | state deltas | everyone's inputs |
| Cheating resistance | none | strong | medium (hash checks) |
| Late join | cached events | snapshot | journal tail / checkpoint |
| Typical use | lobbies, turn-based, co-op, chat-like traffic | shooters, MMO-lite, anything server-authoritative | RTS, fighting, physics sims, anything that must replay bit-exactly |

All modes share: WebSocket control channel, QUIC/WebTransport data path (WebSocket tunnel
when UDP is blocked), three channels (unreliable-sequenced, reliable-ordered,
reliable-unordered), rooms/lobby/properties/master client, grants and quotas.

## relay

Create with `mode: "relay"` (default). Events are opaque bytes with a code, a target
(`all`, `others`, `master`, explicit actors), an optional interest group and a cache flag so
late joiners receive them. Rate and size limits come from the project quota.

Room props `player_ttl_secs` (default 30) and `empty_ttl_secs` (default 5) set how long a
disconnected player keeps their slot and how long an empty room stays open (both capped at
300). Interest groups are `u16` (65 535 groups). A player who connects again while still online
takes over their own slot; the old session gets `left` with reason `session_replaced` and is
ignored from then on.
`cleanup_cache_on_leave` (default true) drops a player's cached events when they leave for good; set it
to false to keep them for late joiners ("keep the cache on leave").
Cache slices: the `cache_slice{op, index?}` control message stamps events
cached from then on — `increase` opens the next slice, `set` picks one, `purge` drops the events of
one slice, `purge_up_to` every slice up to and including `index` (e.g. per-round state a late
joiner no longer needs). Late joiners receive the remaining slices in original order.

Rate limits: a room takes `max_events_per_sec_per_room` events (default 2000) and each player
`max_events_per_sec_per_player` (default 60, burst of 2 s worth); over the limit the event is
dropped with `rate_limited`. Both are project quotas (`/v1/operator/projects/:id/limits`).

### Lobby statistics and presence

`stats` answers with the project's live rooms and players and the same counts per lobby, where a room's
lobby is its room prop `lobby` (always part of the lobby listing; rooms without it form the default lobby
`""`) — lobby statistics without subscribing to the room list. `find_friends{players}` (≤ 64 ids)
answers with `online` (an authenticated control session or a room slot on any node of the fleet) and the
room/node each player is in — find friends. Both fan out across the fleet, so a session may
send at most one per second. Player ids are whatever your grants carry: a friends list itself stays in
your backend.

## sync

Create with `mode: "sync"` and optional props:

| prop | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tick_hz` | 60 | simulation rate (8..128) |
| `schema` | built-in arena | IDL text, see below |
| `budget_bytes` | 1100 | max delta payload per client per tick |
| `aoi_cell`, `aoi_radius` | 32, 2 | interest grid cell size (world units) and radius in cells; `aoi_cell: 0` disables AOI |
| `stale_after` | 30 | ticks after which an entity not sent to a client gets top priority regardless of distance (eventual consistency bound) |
| `position` | `Transform.0` | `Component.field` holding the vec3 used for AOI |

Clients send `Input` frames (last 3 ticks, redundant) on the unreliable channel; the server
runs the simulation, replicates per-client deltas (change masks per component, baselines per
client, priority by change/distance/staleness) and keeps a hitbox history for lag
compensation. Simulation events reach clients on the reliable channel. Every 5 s the frame is
checkpointed to Redis for re-hosting.

Without a `schema` the room runs the built-in arena logic (one avatar per actor, input =
`i8 move_x, i8 move_z, u8 buttons`). With a `schema` and no `logic` the room is
owner-authoritative: each actor owns its avatar entity and its input is a list of full component
writes that the server applies and replicates. An input starting with `0xFF` is instead a list
of ops on entities the actor owns — `write` (any owned entity), `spawn` (a new owned entity,
at most 32 per actor, with initial writes), `despawn`, `transfer` (hand ownership to another
actor in the room; the new owner shows up in the next delta) — so a client can own several
objects (projectiles, pickups, vehicles) and pass them around; a leaving actor's entities are
despawned. With `logic`, the WASM module decides what inputs mean (below).

Deltas go over `UnreliableSequenced`; the client acks every delta (`0x13`: last tick + 32-bit
history, `net_replication::AckTracker`). A delta the client never got has its entities forgotten
on the server, so the next delta carries them in full instead of a diff against state the client
does not have; lost despawns are repeated. Clients that never ack get the plain "baseline = last
sent" behaviour.

Input frames are limited per client to tick rate + 10 % (burst of 8 frames); inputs more than
64 ticks ahead of the room are dropped. Counters: `net_sync_inputs_rate_limited_total`,
`net_sync_invalid_inputs_total`.

### Schema IDL

```text
component Transform {
    pos: vec3 @range(-4096, 4096, 0.01)   // quantized, 3 x 20 bits
    rot: quat                             // smallest-three, 32 bits
    speed: f32                            // raw float
}
component Health {
    hp: u8
    team: i16
    name: string(24)
    flags: bits(5)
}
```

Component flags go on the header line: `component Inventory @owner_only { ... }` is sent only
to the entity's owner (hidden information stays on the server), `component Score @global { ... }`
makes any entity carrying it relevant to everyone regardless of AOI. AOI itself: up to 4
viewpoints per client (the avatar + extras set with the `set_view{viewpoints, interest}` control
message — camera, scope target; spectators get their first viewpoint from it), `interest` forces up
to 64 entities into view regardless of distance (team mates, objectives), and an entity already in
view stays until it is one cell further out than the radius (hysteresis against flicker).

Types: `bool`, `u8..u64`, `i8..i64`, `bits(n)`, `f32`, `f32 @range(min,max,res)`,
`vec2`/`vec3 @range(...)`, `quat`, `string(max)`, `bytes(max)`. The blake3 hash of the
canonical schema is returned in `joined.schema_hash`; a client that sends a different
`schema_hash` on join is refused with `schema_mismatch`.

### Server-side game logic (WASM)

Set `props.logic` to the name of a module uploaded with `PUT /v1/modules/:name` and the
node runs it as the room's authoritative logic: `aurix_join` spawns the avatar,
`aurix_step` reads this tick's inputs and writes components, `raise` sends game events,
`hitbox` feeds lag compensation. Any language that targets wasm32 works; the ABI is plain
integers and floats (see `net-game`). Fuel and memory are capped per call/room, so one
broken game cannot stall a shared node. Without `logic`, a custom schema runs
owner-authoritative (clients write their own entities' components) and no schema at all runs
the built-in arena.

## lockstep

Create with `mode: "lockstep"` and `tick_hz`. The server is the clock: every tick it bundles
the inputs it received for that tick and sends the bundle (plus the two previous ones) to
every actor. Clients simulate with `net-rollback`: predict missing inputs with the actor's
last one, rewind and resimulate when a late input differs, hash the state every N ticks and
report it (`Hash` frame). The server compares hashes per tick; a minority is reported to
everyone as `desync`. The server keeps the canonical input journal, which is also the replay
format (`net-rollback::Replay`): seed + schema hash + inputs per tick reproduces the game.

Use `net-fpmath` (Q32.32 fixed point, table trig, deterministic RNG) for anything that
touches game state; never floats.

### Server-verified lockstep

Give a lockstep room the same `logic` module (and `schema`) a sync room would use and the node
steps it too, over the canonical input journal. Then the node's state hash is the truth: a
client whose hash differs is desynced even if every client agrees with it, checkpoints for
late join and failover come from the node (no master upload), and after a node failover the
new node resimulates the journal tail from the last checkpoint. Clients that want to be
compared must follow the same rule: an actor's avatar spawns at the first tick it appears in a
bundle, state is a `net-sim` frame, hash = `hash_bytes(frame.snapshot())` every 10 ticks.
On a desync the node stores its own state at that tick as the reference dump (actor `0` in
`GET /v1/rooms/:id/desyncs`) next to the desynced client's, so nobody has to trust the master;
room details report `referee: true` while the node hosts such a room. A desynced client is sent a
catch-up (checkpoint + journal tail) for its first three strikes; from the fourth it is `untrusted`
and no longer resynced, so a client lying about its hash cannot make the node re-send the state
every few ticks.

`crates/net-sim-guest` is the reference module for this: `physics-arena`, avatars as fixed-point
circles in a walled `net-sim-physics` world (input = i8 move_x, i8 move_z), built with
`cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p net-sim-guest` and uploaded via
`aurix-net module-put physics-arena target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/net_sim_guest.wasm`.
Clients running the same `net-sim-wasm` physics hash identically to the node.

### Late join and rejoin

A lockstep room never stops for a joiner and never migrates a host. Every
`CHECKPOINT_EVERY_SECS` (5 s) the server asks the master for its newest *confirmed* state
(`CheckpointReq` on the reliable channel; the master answers with `Checkpoint`: tick, hash,
<= 60 KiB of state — use `Rollback::confirmed_state()`). When a data link attaches to a room
that is past tick 0 (late join, or a reconnect into an offline slot) the server sends, on the
reliable-ordered channel, `Catchup` (the newest checkpoint, or tick 0 with an empty state
meaning "start from the seed") followed by every journal bundle from that tick up to the
current one, in ~32 KiB frames. Live bundles keep flowing unreliably in parallel, so the
client buffers them until the reliable tail reaches a tick the live stream already covers
(the tail always overlaps thanks to bundle redundancy). `joined.tick` and `joined.seed` tell
the client where it enters. Start the client with `Rollback::from_checkpoint(cfg, actors,
tick, state)` and feed the tail bundles as confirmed inputs. If a joiner had to replay from a
stale checkpoint the server asks the master for a fresh one at once, so catch-up stays bounded.

## Spectators

`join{name, spectator: true}` watches a room without taking a slot: spectators are not counted
against `max_players`, never become master and cannot send events or inputs (`forbidden`).
Relay: they receive events like everyone else. Sync: they get a view of the whole world (no
AOI, no avatar). Lockstep: they get the input stream `spectator_delay_secs` (room prop, default
3) late, and catch-up only up to that delayed tick, so a streamer's viewers cannot feed live
positions back. `player_joined.player.spectator` tells clients who is watching.

## Node failure: rooms move, they do not die

Every 5 s a node writes each sync/lockstep room to Redis (`net:<project>:ckpt:<room>`, TTL
10 min): the player list (actor ids, player ids, names, master), the simulation snapshot for
sync, and for lockstep the newest master checkpoint plus the input journal from that tick.
When a node misses three heartbeats the others mark its rooms `orphaned` instead of closing
them. The first node a player of that room reaches (plain `join` / `join_or_create` by name
on any node of the region) atomically adopts the row, rebuilds the room from the DB config,
restores the simulation from the checkpoint, recreates every player as an offline slot (so
reconnects get the same actor ids, `rejoin_actor` works) and restarts the tick loop. Lockstep
joiners then get the normal catch-up; sync clients get fresh baselines. Lockstep rooms also
append every tick's input bundle to a Redis list (`net:<project>:journal:<room>`, flushed every
6 ticks), and the adopting node replays the entries after the checkpoint, so at most ~100 ms of
inputs are lost; sync rooms checkpoint every 2 s. A `room.rehosted` webhook fires; orphans nobody adopts within
10 min are closed. Relay rooms are re-created with name/props/slots but no event cache.

## Data frames (first byte)

| kind | direction | mode |
|---|---|---|
| event frame (no kind byte, see `net-rooms::EventFrame`) | both | relay, sync events |
| `0x10` Input | client -> server | sync, lockstep |
| `0x11` Delta | server -> client | sync |
| `0x12` Resync | client -> server | sync |
| `0x13` Ack (last delta tick + 32-bit history) | client -> server | sync |
| `0x20` InputBundle | server -> client | lockstep |
| `0x21` Hash | client -> server | lockstep |
| `0x22` Checkpoint | master -> server (reliable) | lockstep |
| `0x23` CheckpointReq | server -> master (reliable) | lockstep |
| `0x24` Catchup | server -> joiner (reliable), then `0x20` bundles | lockstep |

```

`docs/release-checklist.md`:

```md
# Self-host release checklist

What to do, in order, to put an Aurix Net deployment into production or roll a new version out.
Each step points at the document that explains it; nothing here is optional unless marked.

## Before the first deploy

1. **Secrets** — generate `GRANT_SECRET` (≥ 32 random bytes), `ADMIN_TOKEN`, `METRICS_TOKEN`,
   `PG_PASSWORD`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` (`openssl rand -hex 32`) into a `.env` with mode 600, outside
   the repo. The node refuses to start in `production` with a short or `dev-only` grant secret
   ([deployment.md → Configuration](deployment.md#configuration)).
2. **Network** — Postgres/Redis on the internal network only; TLS terminated in front of
   `8090/tcp` (`deploy/Caddyfile.example`); `7000/udp` + `7443/udp` straight to the nodes with
   their own certificate; proxy ranges in `server.trusted_proxies`; `/metrics` behind
   `METRICS_TOKEN` ([Network](deployment.md#network)).
3. **Image** — tag the commit whose `CHANGELOG.md` has the entry and whose version fields match
   (`Cargo.toml` workspace, `sdk/web`, `sdk/unity`, `dashboard` package.json); build
   `aurix-net:<tag>` from it (`docker build .`), scan it
   (`trivy image aurix-net:<tag>`; CI fails on CRITICAL with a fix), keep the `sbom` artifact
   of that CI run with the release. Pushing the tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which
   checks the version fields against the tag, builds the linux x86_64/aarch64 server bundles
   (node, CLI, loadtest, `libaurix_net` + headers), the Web npm tarball, the Unity/Godot/C++
   archives, the SBOM, multi-arch `ghcr.io/<org>/aurix-net:<tag>` and `aurix-net-console:<tag>`
   images (CRITICAL-with-fix gate) and attaches everything with SHA-256 sums to a GitHub Release.
4. **Compose** — copy `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`, set `PUBLIC_HOST` per node and
   `REGION`, point the console's `NET_API_URL` at the load balancer, keep `read_only`,
   `cap_drop`, `no-new-privileges`, `nofile`, log rotation and `stop_grace_period: 30s`.
5. **Migrate** — `docker compose run --rm node-a --migrate-only` once, then `up -d`
   ([Migrations](deployment.md#migrations)).
6. **Verify** — `/healthz` 200 on every node and via the proxy; `GET /v1/operator/nodes` lists
   all nodes with the right region; create a project + key, create a room with REST, join it with
   an SDK client through the proxy (WebSocket) and natively (QUIC); open the console.
7. **Monitoring** — `--profile monitoring up -d` or scrape `/metrics` from your Prometheus;
   load `deploy/monitoring/alerts.yml` (node down, slow ticks, overruns, desyncs, auth brute
   force, Redis write errors, rooms near cap) ([Monitoring](deployment.md#monitoring)).
8. **Backups** — schedule `scripts/backup.sh` (cron, off-host copy) and run one restore drill
   into a scratch database before go-live ([Backups](deployment.md#backups)).

## Every release

1. Read the release notes for config changes; nodes of one deployment run the same minor version.
2. Build + scan the image; `--migrate-only` with the new image while the old nodes keep serving.
   Exception, once: upgrading across migration `0012` (adds `nodes.heartbeat_secs`) — restart the old nodes
   right after migrating; their node-registry queries used `SELECT *` and fail with
   `cached plan must not change result type` until reconnect. From 0012 on these queries name their columns.
3. Rolling restart one node at a time, waiting for `/healthz` 200 before the next
   ([Upgrades](deployment.md#upgrades)); rooms are checkpointed and adopted by the other nodes,
   players reconnect by room name.
4. Watch `aurix_sync_tick_p99`, overruns, desync and auth-rejection counters for 15 minutes.
5. Roll back by redeploying the previous image; schema changes are additive, so the previous
   version runs against the migrated database. Restore from backup only if data was corrupted.

## Periodically

- Rotate secrets per the table in [Secrets and rotation](deployment.md#secrets-and-rotation);
  grant-secret rotation is zero-downtime via `auth.grant_secret_previous`.
- Rebuild the image when the distroless base or Rust dependencies get security updates
  (`cargo audit` / `cargo deny` run in CI on every push).
- Review `GET /v1/operator/audit` and per-project limits/quotas; prune expired API keys.
- Run a restore drill from a real backup.

```

`docs/sdk.md`:

```md
# SDKs

| SDK | Path | Transport | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rust | `crates/net-client` | QUIC + WS tunnel | verified (`examples/relay_echo`) |
| C ABI | `crates/net-ffi` (`libaurix_net`, `include/aurix_net.h`) | via Rust client | verified (`ctest/echo.c`) |
| C ABI, aurix-sim | `libaurix_net` also exports `sim_*`/`sim3_*` (`include/aurix_sim.h`, copies in `sdk/cpp`, `sdk/godot/src`) | native | verified (`ctest/sim.c`: six golden hashes) |
| C++ (header-only) | `sdk/cpp/aurix_net.hpp` | via C ABI: relay, sync (`aurix::net::Sync`), lockstep | verified (`echo_test.cpp`, `sync_test.cpp`) |
| Unity (UPM) | `sdk/unity` | pure C# (WebSocket control + tunnel), optional P/Invoke QUIC | managed core live-tested with dotnet; `NetRunner`/`NetView`/`NetTransform`/`[Sync]`/`[Rpc]`, `LockstepClient` + editor window written, real editor build pending; `NetRigidbody`/`NetAnimator`/`TickTimer`/`ISpawned`/`IDespawned` compile-checked (BuildCheck), editor run pending a license |
| Godot 4 GDExtension | `sdk/godot` | C++ wrapper over C ABI | verified (godot-cpp 4.2 build, headless Godot 4.2.2 relay + sync replication: `sdk/godot/check~`) |
| Web (`@aurix/net`) | `sdk/web` | WS control + WS tunnel (WebTransport next) | verified (`npm test`) |

All SDKs share one shape: `connect(http, grant)` → `joinOrCreate/join` → per frame `poll()`,
`sendEvent/sendData`, `flush()`; events `control` (JSON), `event` (relay frame), `data` (raw
sync/lockstep frames), `closed`. Grants always come from the developer's backend.

## Rehost

When a node shuts down (deploy) it hands its rooms to another node and sends `left{reason:"rehost"}`. Clients rejoin the same room with the same grant: Rust `client.rejoin(&[fallback_urls])`, Web `client.rejoin(fallbackUrls)` (or listen to the `rehost` event), C# `ManagedClient.RejoinAsync(fallbacks)`; Unity `NetRunner` does it automatically (`FallbackUrls`). Actor ids are preserved by player id.

## Lobby statistics and presence

lobby statistics and find-friends, one control round-trip each (at most one per second per
session, both fan out across the fleet):

- Web: `await client.lobbyStats()` → `{rooms, players, lobbies: [{lobby, rooms, players}]}`;
  `await client.findFriends(["ann", "bob"])` → `[{player, online, room?: {id, name, mode, node}}]`.
- Unity (managed): `await client.StatsAsync()` / `await client.FindFriendsAsync(new[]{"ann","bob"})` return
  the JSON answers (`Json.Str/Num/Obj` helpers read them).
- Rust: `client.stats().await?` / `client.find_friends(vec![...]).await?`; the answers arrive as
  `Event::Control(ServerMsg::Stats { .. })` / `ServerMsg::Friends { .. }`.
- One-shot room list and WebRPC: Web `await client.rooms("map = 'dust'")` / `await client.rpc("inventory.get", {slot: 3})`
  → `{ok, status, body, error?}`; Unity `RoomsAsync(expr)` / `RpcAsync(name, bodyJson)`; Rust
  `client.rpc(id, name, body)` with the answer as `ServerMsg::RpcResult { id, .. }`. `rpc` reaches the
  project's webhook subscribed to `rpc` (docs/api.md → Webhooks); the client never sees its URL.

A room's lobby is its room prop `lobby` (always visible in listings); rooms without one form the default
lobby `""`. See docs/modes.md.

## Lockstep rooms from Rust, C++ and Godot

`net_client::lockstep::LockstepClient` is the same core the C# and Web SDKs use, as pure logic: feed
every data-path payload to `receive()` and act on the events it returns (`Tick` with the confirmed
inputs in tick order, `Restore` on catch-up, `CheckpointRequested` for the master, `DumpRequested`
after a desync); send what `send_input()`, `hash_frame()`, `checkpoint_frame()` and `dump_frame()`
hand back (`Outgoing::reliable` picks the channel). Input delay adapts to the node's margin reports
(`0x25`) between `input_delay_min/max`; `input_redundancy` (1–8) past inputs ride in every datagram.

The C ABI mirrors it (`aurix_net_lockstep_*` in `aurix_net.h`) and the header-only
`aurix::net::Lockstep` wraps it for C++ and the Godot extension:

```cpp
aurix::net::Client c; c.connect(http, grant);
c.joinOrCreate("duel", aurix::net::Mode::Lockstep, 2);
aurix::net::Lockstep ls;
// per frame
ls.sendInput(c, input, sizeof input);
c.poll(); // for each Data event: if (!ls.receive(ev.data, ev.len)) handleRelay(ev);
for (auto e = ls.poll(); e.kind != aurix::net::Lockstep::Kind::None; e = ls.poll()) {
  switch (e.kind) {
    case aurix::net::Lockstep::Kind::Tick:    sim.step(e.tick, e.inputs); aurix::net::Lockstep::reportHash(c, e.tick, sim.hash()); break;
    case aurix::net::Lockstep::Kind::Restore: sim.restore(e.state, e.stateLen); break;
    case aurix::net::Lockstep::Kind::CheckpointReq: aurix::net::Lockstep::sendCheckpoint(c, e.tick, sim.hash(), sim.bytes(), sim.size()); break;
    case aurix::net::Lockstep::Kind::DumpReq: aurix::net::Lockstep::sendDump(c, e.tick, sim.hashAt(e.tick), sim.bytesAt(e.tick), sim.sizeAt(e.tick)); break;
    default: break;
  }
}
```

## Sync rooms from C++ and Godot

`aurix_net_sync_*` (in `aurix_net.h`) is the client side of a sync room as pure logic: a replicated
world (`net_sim::Frame` + the same delta decoder the node uses), acks, redundant input frames and
owner-authoritative component writes. `aurix::net::Sync` wraps it:

```cpp
aurix::net::Client c; c.connect(http, grant);
c.joinOrCreate("arena", aurix::net::Mode::Sync, 8, "{\"schema\":" + aurix::net::Client::quote(SCHEMA) + "}");
aurix::net::Sync world(SCHEMA, 60, 2);
int tr = world.component("Transform"), pos = world.field(tr, "pos");
c.onData = [&](auto, auto, const uint8_t* d, size_t n) { world.receive(c, d, n); }; // applies + acks
// per frame:
c.poll(); world.advance(dt);
for (auto e = world.poll(); e.kind != aurix::net::Sync::Kind::None; e = world.poll()) {
    float p[4]; if (world.vector(e.entity, tr, pos, p) == 3) { /* spawn/change/despawn of e.entity */ }
}
float mine[3] = {x, y, z};
world.begin(tr).write(pos, mine, 3).end().sendWrites(c);   // owner-authoritative rooms
world.begin(tr).write(pos, mine, 3).end().spawn(c);        // a second entity you own; despawn/transfer/writeEntity likewise
// world.sendInput(c, bytes, n) for rooms with server-side `logic`
// Web: session.spawn(writes) / writeEntity(id, writes) / despawn(id) / transfer(id, actor); C#: SyncWorld.EncodeOps(SyncOp[...])
```

Godot: `AurixNetSync` (RefCounted) — `setup(schema)`, feed the client's `data` signal to
`receive(client, payload)`, listen to `spawn(entity, owner)` / `change` / `despawn`, read
`get_field(entity, "Transform", "pos")` as Vector3/Quaternion/float/String, write with
`begin_write("Transform")`, `write_field("pos", Vector3(...))`, `end_write()`, `send_writes(client)`.
`sdk/cpp/sync_test.cpp` is the live check (two clients, writes replicate, no gaps).

## Predict/rollback on lockstep (zero-lag local input)

Plain lockstep renders a tick only once the node has confirmed everybody's input, so local actions
show up `input_delay` ticks late. The rollback runner removes that: the game runs ahead of the
confirmed tick with *predicted* inputs (every remote actor's last confirmed input repeated, your own
inputs exactly as sent), keeps a snapshot per predicted tick, and when a confirmed tick differs from
the prediction it restores the snapshot, re-steps that tick and re-predicts the ticks after it. The
confirmed state only ever sees confirmed inputs, so determinism and hash reports are untouched.

Same core in three SDKs: `net_client::rollback::Rollback<S: Simulation>` (Rust),
`LockstepRollback<S>` + `Simulation<S>` (Web), `LockstepRollback<TSnapshot>` + `ISimulation<TSnapshot>`
(C#). Your simulation implements `step(tick, inputs)`, `snapshot()`, `restore(snapshot)`; keep
snapshots cheap (value copies of the game state) because one is taken per predicted tick.

```ts
const ls = new LockstepClient((ch, p) => c.sendData(ch, p));
const rb = new LockstepRollback(game, joined.actor, 0, 8);   // up to 8 predicted ticks
ls.onTick = (t, inputs) => { rb.confirm(t, inputs); ls.reportHash(t, hashOf(rb.confirmedSnapshot())); };
ls.onRestore = (t, _h, state) => { game.load(state); rb.reset(t); };
// per frame
const tick = ls.sendInput(input); rb.localInput(tick, input);
rb.predict(ls.serverTick + ls.inputDelay);                    // run up to where our input will land
render(game);                                                 // predicted state, no input lag
```

Rollback counters (`rollbacks`, `resimulatedTicks`, `predictedTicks`) tell you how often remote
players change their input unexpectedly; a high ratio means lower `maxPrediction` or smoothing in
the view. Hash reports must be computed on the *confirmed* state (`confirmedSnapshot()` after `confirm`),
never on the predicted head — the head is speculative and differs between players.

## Instant replay (kill cam)

Two ways to rewind a lockstep match:

- **Locally, no round trip** — `ReplayRing` (Rust `net_client::rollback::ReplayRing`, Web/C# `ReplayRing`)
  keeps the last `keep` confirmed ticks' inputs and a snapshot of the confirmed state every `every`
  ticks. Record from the confirmed path, then `window(from)` gives the nearest snapshot at or before
  `from` and the inputs to step from it:

  ```ts
  const ring = new ReplayRing(300, 10);           // 10 s at 30 Hz, snapshot every 10 ticks
  ls.onTick = (t, inputs) => { const before = rb.confirmedSnapshot(); rb.confirm(t, inputs); ring.record(t, inputs, () => before); };
  // kill cam: last 3 s
  const w = ring.window(rb.confirmedTick - 90);
  if (w) { cam.restore(w.snapshot); let t = w.start; for (const i of w.inputs) cam.step(t++, i); }
  ```

- **From the node** — `GET /v1/rooms/:id/replay?from=&to=` returns the confirmed inputs of a *live*
  room from whichever node hosts it (and windows the stored replay after close). Use it for
  spectators who arrived late, bug reports and server-side highlight generation; the payload is the
  same `Replay` JSON as the post-match replay (`from_tick`, `inputs`, `hashes`).


## Aurix Sim — deterministic physics in every SDK

`net-sim-physics` (fixed-point Q32.32, no floats) is exposed through one flat ABI crate,
`net-sim-wasm`, built both as `net_sim_wasm.wasm` (browsers, Unity WebGL, node referee) and as a
native `libnet_sim_wasm.{so,dll,dylib}` (Unity desktop/mobile, C++/Godot). Every build runs the
same integer math, so a lockstep room can hash the world on any platform and compare:
`sim_golden_hash()` returns `0x58d9870ba45952b5` on x86-64 native and wasm32.

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p net-sim-wasm   # target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/net_sim_wasm.wasm
cargo build --release -p net-sim-wasm                                   # target/release/libnet_sim_wasm.so
cargo run -p net-sim-wasm --example golden_check                        # native vs wasm hash
```

Web:

```ts
import { Sim, BodyKind } from "@aurix/net";
const sim = await Sim.load(fetch("/net_sim_wasm.wasm"));
const w = sim.world({ x: 0, y: -10 }, 60);
w.addBox(BodyKind.Static, 0, -1, 50, 1);
const hero = w.addCapsule(BodyKind.Kinematic, 0, 1, 0.5, 0.5);
const kcc = w.character(hero);            // step-up 0.5, slope limit cos 0.7
const ball = w.addCircle(BodyKind.Dynamic, 3, 5, 0.5);
w.setMaterial(ball, 0.3, 0.6);
// per lockstep tick:
w.moveCharacter(kcc, input.x / 60, vy / 60);
w.step();
lockstep.reportHash(tick, w.hash());      // identical on every client
const snap = w.snapshot();                // for rollback / checkpoints
```

Unity (C#): `Aurix.Net.Sim.SimWorld` has the same surface (`AddBox/AddCircle/AddCapsule`,
`SetMaterial/SetLayers/SetVelocity/ApplyImpulse`, `Body(id)`, `Raycast`, `Character/MoveCharacter`,
`Snapshot/Restore/Hash`). Put `libnet_sim_wasm.so`/`.dll` under `Plugins/` (WebGL links the static
build). Rust games use `net-sim-physics` directly (`World`, `Body`, `Joint`, `CharacterController`),
with joints (distance/rope, revolute with limits and motor, weld) and contact events on top of what
the flat ABI exposes today.

Navigation rides on the same module (`net-sim-nav`): `navGrid`/`navLoad` (JSON from
`NavMesh::to_bytes`), `navPath` (A* over portals + funnel), `navRaycast` (line of sight),
`navField` (one flow field per goal, shared by any number of agents), `addAgent`/`agentTarget`/
`agentFollow`, `crowdStep` next to `step()`, `crowdHash`/`crowdSnapshot` for lockstep checks.
C#: `NavGrid/NavLoad/NavPath/NavRaycast/NavField/AddAgent/AgentTarget/AgentFollow/CrowdStep`.
Reference hash `sim_nav_golden_hash()` = `0x746c5a608abe2f26` on native and wasm32.

```ts
w.navGrid({ x: 0, y: 0 }, 1, 64, 64, blockedCells);
const toBase = w.navField({ x: 60.5, y: 60.5 });
const unit = w.addAgent(2, 2, 0.4, 3);
w.agentFollow(unit, toBase);
// per tick: w.crowdStep(); w.step(); lockstep.reportHash(tick, w.hash() ^ w.crowdHash());
```

Joints, contact events and shape casts are on the same handle: `jointDistance` (rope when
`minLength < length`), `jointRevolute` (limits + motor, `setMotor` to retune), `jointWeld`,
`removeJoint`; `events()` returns the begin/end contact pairs of the last `step()`; `circleCast`
sweeps a circle and reports where it first touches (C#: `JointDistance/JointRevolute/JointWeld/
RemoveJoint/SetMotor/Events/CircleCast`). Reference hash `sim_joint_golden_hash()` =
`0x4bcc781a484ceeed` on native and wasm32.

### 3D worlds

The same module hosts `net-sim-physics3d`: `sim.world3(gravity, hz)` → `Sim3World` with
`addSphere/addBox/addCapsule`, `setMaterial/setLayers/setVelocity/setPosition/setRotation`
(`Sim3World.axisAngle` builds quaternions), `applyImpulse(id, impulse, at?)`, `body(id)`
(position, rotation, velocity, angular velocity), `raycast`, `events`, `snapshot/restore/hash`.
C#: `Aurix.Net.Sim.Sim3World` with the same surface (`Vec3`, `Quat.AxisAngle`, `Body3State`,
`Ray3Hit`). Reference hash `sim3_golden_hash()` = `0x0a9c7e6fc4fa43bf` on native and wasm32.

```ts
const w3 = sim.world3();
w3.addBox(BodyKind.Static, { x: 0, y: -0.5, z: 0 }, { x: 50, y: 0.5, z: 50 });
const crate = w3.addBox(BodyKind.Dynamic, { x: 0, y: 3, z: 0 }, { x: 0.5, y: 0.5, z: 0.5 });
w3.setRotation(crate, Sim3World.axisAngle({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 1 }, 0.3));
// per tick: w3.step(); lockstep.reportHash(tick, w3.hash());
```

3D joints and characters: `jointBall`, `jointHinge` (local axes, optional limits + motor,
`hingeAngle`, `setMotor`), `jointDistance` (rope when `minLength < length`), `removeJoint`;
`character(body)` wraps a kinematic capsule in a controller — `moveCharacter(k, delta)` before
`step()` slides along geometry, steps over ledges up to `stepHeight`, snaps to the ground and
reports `characterState(k).grounded`. C#: `JointBall/JointHinge/JointDistance/HingeAngle/
Character/MoveCharacter/CharacterState`. Reference hash `sim3_joint_golden_hash()` =
`0x5db56af63cceee85` on native and wasm32.

Bot kit ports: Web `BehaviorTree/StateMachine/Blackboard` (`sdk/web/src/bots.ts`) and C#
`Aurix.Net.Sim.Bots` load the same JSON as the Rust `net-sim-bots` crate and produce identical
per-tick statuses and hashes — verified against `crates/net-sim-bots/fixtures/vectors.json`
(regenerate with `BOTS_WRITE_VECTORS=1 cargo test -p net-sim-bots vectors`).

3D convex hulls and sweeps: `addConvex(kind, pos, verts, faces)` / C# `AddConvex` build a convex
polyhedron from <= 32 body-space vertices and faces given as index loops (winding is normalised,
author vertices around the centre of mass; mass is exact volume, inertia the bounding box) — hulls
collide with spheres, capsules, boxes and each other via SAT over face normals and edge crosses with
reference-face clipping. `sphereCast(from, dir, radius)` / `SphereCast` sweeps a sphere and reports
the first body, the centre's stop fraction and the surface point/normal. Reference hash
`sim3_hull_golden_hash()` = `0xd656fc8f55999cf8` on native and wasm32. `capsuleCast(from, rot, halfLen, radius, dir)` / `boxCast(from, rot, half, dir)` (Unity `CapsuleCast`/`BoxCast`, C ABI `sim3_capsulecast`/`sim3_boxcast`) sweep a rotated capsule (local axis Y) or box the same way and return the same hit shape.

### aurix-sim from C / C++ / Godot

`libaurix_net` (crates/net-ffi) links `net-sim-wasm`, so the same flat ABI the Web and Unity
wrappers use is callable natively: `include/aurix_sim.h` (generated by `tools/gen_sim_header.py`,
96 functions: `sim_*` 2D physics/joints/casts, `sim_nav_*`/`sim_agent_*`/`sim_crowd_*` navigation,
`sim3_*` 3D physics/joints/character/convex hulls/sphere casts, and the six `*_golden_hash()`
scenes). Values are raw Q32.32 (`aurix_fx_from_double`/`aurix_fx_to_double`); handles and ids are
the same numbers the Web/Unity wrappers pass through. A GDExtension can call it directly from
`aurix_net_client.cpp`'s neighbourhood (header copied to `sdk/godot/src`); `crates/net-ffi/ctest/sim.c`
is the offline check (golden hashes + a resting ball in 2D and 3D + a sphere cast).

```

`docs/sim/design.md`:

```md
# aurix-sim — deterministic simulation kit (design)

Goal: a deterministic gameplay
engine that runs identically on every client (native and WASM) and, when wanted, on the node as a
referee. It stays a library the game links, not a service: lockstep transport, hashes, desync dumps,
rollback (`net_client::rollback`) and replays already exist; aurix-sim gives games something
deterministic to run on top of them without writing their own fixed-point physics.

Non-goals (for now): 3D rigid-body physics (phase 3), rendering/animation, a visual bot editor.

## Building blocks already in the repo

| Crate | Reused for |
|---|---|
| `net-fpmath` | `Fx` (Q32.32), `FxVec2/3`, `FxRng`, integer-only sqrt/trig |
| `net-sim` | `Frame`: entities, schema components, per-actor inputs, events, snapshot/restore/hash |
| `net-rollback` (server) / `net_client::rollback` | predict/rollback loops |
| `net-game` | WASM sandbox on the node (referee runs, server-side bots) |

## Phase 1 — `net-sim-physics` (2D)

Deterministic 2D rigid bodies in fixed point, API shaped after Box2D but without floats:

- **World**: gravity, fixed `dt = 1/tick_hz` (`Fx`), substeps, `step(&mut self)`; everything
  ordered by stable ids (`BodyId(u32)`, `ShapeId(u32)`) — no HashMap iteration, no pointers.
- **Bodies**: static / kinematic / dynamic; position, rotation (`Fx` angle, cached sin/cos in Fx),
  linear/angular velocity, mass/inertia from shapes, damping, bullet flag, sleep.
- **Shapes**: circle, capsule, convex polygon (≤ 8 vertices), edge chain for terrain; density,
  friction, restitution (combine: max friction, min restitution — overridable), collision
  layers/masks (`u32`), sensor flag.
- **Broadphase**: uniform grid (cell size = 2 × largest shape) with deterministic pair ordering
  (sorted by `(min_id, max_id)`), rebuilt incrementally; no SAP/float tree.
- **Narrowphase**: circle–circle, circle–polygon, polygon–polygon (SAT, clipped manifold ≤ 2 points),
  capsule via segment distance; manifold ids keyed on feature pairs for warm starting.
- **Solver**: sequential impulses, 8 velocity / 3 position iterations (configurable), Baumgarte +
  slop, restitution threshold, warm starting with accumulated impulses stored in the manifold;
  iteration order = sorted contact keys so every machine applies impulses in the same order.
- **Joints**: distance, revolute (with limits/motor), prismatic, weld, mouse/target — same solver.
- **Queries**: `raycast`, `shapecast`, `overlap_aabb/circle/polygon`, point test; results sorted by
  `(fraction, id)`.
- **Character controller (KCC)**: capsule mover with slope limit, step-up, ground snap, push-out;
  deterministic by construction (no engine callbacks).
- **Events**: begin/end contact, sensor enter/exit, collected per step in id order.
- **Snapshot/restore/hash**: whole world is `Clone` + `Serialize` (bytes via `postcard`), hash =
  FNV-1a over the canonical byte form — plugs straight into lockstep hash reports and dumps.
- **Determinism rules**: no `f32/f64` anywhere in the crate (`#![forbid]` via clippy lint
  `float_arithmetic` + a CI grep), no `HashMap` iteration, no `std::time`, no threads; every
  `Fx` op wraps/saturates explicitly.

Tests: unit tests per primitive; **golden-hash scenarios** (pyramid stack, bouncing balls,
ragdoll chain, KCC obstacle course) run N ticks and compare to committed hashes on x86_64, aarch64
and wasm32 (CI matrix) — the same vectors shipped to the C# and TS ports.

## Phase 2 — `net-sim-nav`

- Navmesh import (triangles from any baker: Recast output, Unity NavMesh export, hand-made) into a
  fixed-point mesh with regions and off-mesh links; serialization same as physics.
- A* over triangles + funnel (string pulling) → path of `FxVec2`; corridor refresh when the
  target moves.
- Steering agents: seek/arrive, separation (RVO-lite with deterministic neighbor order), avoidance
  of static obstacles; agent radius classes.
- Flow fields for crowds (per-target grid, integrated once per N ticks).
- Queries: nearest point on mesh, line-of-sight, random point in region.

## Phase 3 — 3D and bot kit

- 3D rigid bodies (sphere, capsule, box, convex hull, static triangle mesh), GJK/EPA in fixed
  point, same solver layout — scope decided after phase 1 numbers.
- Bot kit: deterministic HFSM + behaviour-tree runtime driven from `Frame` inputs, so bot seats
  from matchmaking (`bots`) can be filled by the same code on every client or on the node.

## Bindings

- **Rust**: the crates themselves (`net-sim-physics`, `net-sim-nav`).
- **WASM**: `cdylib` with a flat ABI (ids + Fx as i64) so Web and Unity (WebGL/IL2CPP) load the
  same `.wasm`; a thin TS/C# wrapper mirrors the API. Same bytes = same results everywhere.
- **Native C ABI** via `net-ffi` for C++/Godot.
- Node referee: the WASM build runs inside `net-game` to verify hashes or host bots.

## Milestones

1. `net-sim-physics` world + circles/polygons + grid broadphase + SI solver + raycast, golden
   hashes on native and wasm32.
2. Joints, capsules, edge chains, KCC, contact events; Web/C# wrappers over the WASM build;
   example lockstep game in `examples/`.
3. `net-sim-nav` A*/funnel/steering; flow fields.
4. 3D decision + bot kit.

## Status

- Phase 1 done: bodies (static/kinematic/dynamic), circles, boxes/convex polygons, capsules, edge
  chains; uniform-grid broadphase with sorted pairs; SAT manifolds over rounded convex cores;
  sequential impulses with warm starting, friction, restitution (pre-solve bias), positional
  correction; joints (distance/rope with slack, revolute with limits + motor, weld; jointed bodies
  do not collide); raycast (circle/polygon/capsule/segment); kinematic `CharacterController`
  (slide, step-up, ground snap, slope limit); contact/sensor events; snapshot/restore/FNV hash.
- Bindings: `net-sim-wasm` flat ABI (cdylib + wasm32), Web `Sim/SimWorld`, Unity
  `Aurix.Net.Sim.SimWorld`; golden hash `0x58d9870ba45952b5` identical on native and wasm32.
- Phase 2 done: `net-sim-nav` — convex-polygon navmesh with shared-edge adjacency and a grid
  builder, locate/nearest, A* over portals (BTreeSet frontier), funnel straightening, mesh
  raycast, per-area cost/flags, flow fields (Dijkstra per goal), `Crowd` (arrive, separation,
  sampled velocity-obstacle avoidance, border sliding, depenetration, snapshot/hash); exposed over
  the flat ABI + Web/Unity wrappers; nav golden hash `0x746c5a608abe2f26` native == wasm32.
- Phase 1 leftovers closed: `World::circle_cast` (sweep against shapes inflated by the radius),
  joints/motor retune, contact events and circle cast over the flat ABI + Web/Unity wrappers;
  joint golden hash `0x4bcc781a484ceeed` native == wasm32. Polygon/capsule sweeps are not
  implemented (circle cast covers characters and projectiles).
- Phase 3 (in progress): `net-sim-physics3d` — spheres, capsules, boxes (static/kinematic/
  dynamic), 3D grid broadphase, analytic sphere/capsule contacts, sphere/capsule vs box,
  box-box SAT (15 axes) with reference-face clipping (≤4 points), sequential impulses with warm
  starting, two-axis friction, restitution, positional correction, quaternion integration
  (`FxQuat`/`FxMat3` in net-fpmath), raycasts, snapshot/restore/hash; tests run two worlds and
  compare hashes; exposed as `sim3_*` over the flat ABI with Web `Sim3World` / Unity `Sim3World`
  wrappers, golden hash `0x0a9c7e6fc4fa43bf` native == wasm32. 3D joints (ball,
  hinge with limits/motor, distance/rope, `FxMat3` inverse for the point constraint) and a
  kinematic capsule `CharacterController` (push-out sliding, step-up with ledge probe, ground
  snap, slope filter) are in, exposed over `sim3_joint_*`/`sim3_kcc_*` with Web/Unity wrappers;
  golden hash `0x5db56af63cceee85` native == wasm32. Convex hulls (SAT faces + edge crosses, face clipping, hull pairs with every
  primitive, Cyrus–Beck raycast) and sphere sweeps (`sphere_cast`) are in, exposed as
  `sim3_convex_*`/`sim3_add_convex`/`sim3_spherecast` with Web/Unity wrappers; golden hash
  `0xd656fc8f55999cf8` native == wasm32 (the hash also covers capsule and box sweeps, `shape_cast` over the solver's own contact generators: `capsule_cast`/`box_cast`, ABI `sim3_capsulecast`/`sim3_boxcast`).
- Bot kit: `net-sim-bots` — data-driven behavior trees (Sequence/Selector/Parallel, Condition/
  Action by id via the `Brain` trait, Inverter/Succeeder/Repeat/Cooldown/Timeout/Wait, blackboard
  Compare/Set), hierarchical state machines (parent transitions, on_enter/on_exit, initial
  children), integer `Blackboard`, tick-based timers, JSON authoring, snapshot/hash, and navmesh
  glue (`go_to`, `follow_field`, `stop`, `sync_agent`) over `net-sim-nav` crowds. Ported to
  TS (`sdk/web/src/bots.ts`) and C# (`Aurix.Net.Sim.Bots`), replaying the shared vector fixture.

## Referee module

`net-sim-guest` (`physics-arena`) packages the 2D physics as a room-logic WASM module the node runs as
lockstep referee (see docs/modes.md, "Server-verified lockstep"); the soak in docs/testing.md runs
it under load. Guest memory is not checkpointed across failover — the world is rebuilt from the
frame's `Transform.pos` with zero velocity, which is the documented approximation.

```

`docs/testing.md`:

```md
# Local verification

Everything below runs on one machine against `deploy/docker-compose.dev.yml` (Postgres +
Redis). Build once: `cargo build --release`. Create a project and key with the operator API
(`aurix-net project-create`, needs `NET_OPERATOR_TOKEN` = `NET__AUTH__ADMIN_TOKEN`) and export
`NET_API_KEY`.

| What | Command | Expect |
|---|---|---|
| unit + integration | `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` | green |
| relay load | `aurix-net-loadtest --mode relay --rooms 100 --players 10 --rate 20` | loss < 1%, p99 < 10 ms (release) |
| relay via WebSocket tunnel / WebTransport | add `--tunnel` / `--webtransport` | same, slightly higher latency |
| sync (built-in arena) | `--mode sync --rooms 4 --players 64 --tick-hz 60` | server tick p99 <= 8 ms, ~60 deltas/s/player |
| sync loss repair | `--mode sync --rooms 2 --players 8 --drop-in 0.05` | `client gaps noticed` ≈ dropped deltas, server `net_sync_lost_deltas_total` grows by about the same; no resync, state repaired in full per entity |
| sync with WASM logic | `aurix-net module-put arena crates/net-game/examples/arena.wat`, then `--mode sync --props-json '{"schema": "...", "logic": "arena"}'` | same delta rate as built-in |
| lockstep + late join | `--mode lockstep --rooms 4 --players 4 --late-join-secs 12` | `caught-up = rooms`, no `catch-up gap` |
| node failover | `scripts/two-nodes.sh start`, `scripts/failover-test.sh` | room adopted by B, joiners caught up |
| cross-node matchmaking | file one ticket on :8090 and one on :8091 (same shape, `min_players: 2`) | both `matched` to the same room, readable from either node |
| redirect follow | room on A, `cargo run --release -p net-client --example follow -- http://127.0.0.1:8091 $NET_API_KEY <room>` | joins with data host of A |
| quotas | `UPDATE projects SET limits = '{"max_rooms":1}'`, loadtest `--rooms 2` | second room fails `quota_exceeded: max 1 open rooms` |
| metering | loadtest `--duration-secs 75`, then `aurix-net usage` | room_minutes/player_minutes/bytes rows for the hour |
| browser WebTransport | serve `sdk/web` (`python3 -m http.server 8765`), open `test/browser.html?http=...&ga=<grant>&gb=<grant>&room=x` in Chrome | `path=webtransport/webtransport hello=1 ticks=10/10` |
| Web SDK (Node, tunnel) | `cd sdk/web && NET_API_KEY=... npm test` | pass |
| C / C++ ABI | `crates/net-ffi/ctest/echo.c`, `sdk/cpp/echo_test.cpp` against a live node | `hello=1 ticks=10/10` |
| C ABI, aurix-sim | `crates/net-ffi/ctest/sim.c` against `libaurix_net.so` (offline) | six golden hashes equal to Rust/wasm32, 2D/3D rest + sphere cast |

Known limits of the local setup: bots and server share CPU, so the 2000 events/s/room figure
needs bots on a second machine; the dev certificate changes on every node start (browser pins
the fingerprint from `joined.data`, nothing to install).

## Unity managed client (pure C#)

```
cd sdk/unity/BuildCheck~/managed-live && NET_API_KEY=an_… dotnet run -c Release
```
Expects `MANAGED OK`: 1 reliable, 10 unreliable and one 5 KB fragmented relay event delivered
between two clients, and >60 sync deltas in 2 s. Needs a node on 127.0.0.1:8090 with the tunnel on.

## Rolling deploy (SIGTERM handoff)

```
KILL_SIGNAL=TERM scripts/failover-test.sh
```
Same pass criteria as the crash variant, but node A hands its rooms off itself on SIGTERM
(fresh checkpoint, rooms `orphaned`), so players reconnecting 2 s later already find the room
on B. Clients receive `left{reason:"rehost"}` and should rejoin the same room name
(`connect_and_join` / `connectAndJoin`), which lands on whichever node adopts it.

Client-side check of the same path (Rust SDK `rejoin`): `cargo build --example rehost -p net-client`, run
`target/debug/examples/rehost http://127.0.0.1:8090 <grant> <room> http://127.0.0.1:8091`, send SIGTERM
to node A; expected output ends with `rejoined ... (same actor: true)` and `REHOST_OK`.

SDK side of the same handoff: `NET_API_KEY=... scripts/sdk-rehost-test.sh` puts a Web client and a
pure-C# client in one relay room on A, sends A SIGTERM and expects both to see `left{reason:"rehost"}`,
`rejoin()` / `RejoinAsync()` onto B with the same actor id, and to receive an event from a client that
joins on B afterwards (`WEB_REHOST_OK`, `CS_REHOST_OK`). The Rust client has the same check as
`cargo run -p net-client --example rehost`.

## Redis outage (chaos)

Stop Redis for ~12 s in the middle of a lockstep or sync match (`docker stop aurix-redis`, later
`docker start`): play must continue untouched (tick loops never await Redis), the node logs a few
`redis write failed/timed out` warnings during the outage and none after Redis is back, journal keys
reappear, and the first lockstep tick after a lost journal batch writes a fresh checkpoint (an adopting
node replays the journal only up to the first gap). Verified: 4/4 players, 5 warnings in 12 s, 0 after.

## Postgres outage (chaos)

Stop Postgres for ~12 s mid-match: play continues (no tick loop touches the pool), joins/REST fail
fast (5 s pool acquire timeout) instead of hanging, heartbeats and metering resume on their own, and
rooms that emptied meanwhile still close after `player_ttl` + `empty_ttl`. Verified: sync 8/8 players,
only sqlx "slow acquire" warnings, node healthy afterwards.

## Capacity reference (one 8-core machine, bots and nodes sharing CPU, release build)

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| relay 4 rooms x 32 players @ 20 ev/s, one source IP | 128/128 joined, loss 0.34 %, latency p50 1.8 ms / p99 3.5 ms |
| relay 1 room x 64 players @ 20 ev/s | 64/64 joined, loss 0.49 %, p99 3.4 ms |
| sync 4 x 32 @ 60 Hz | 128/128 joined, server tick mean 0.69 ms, p99 <= 2 ms, ~100 deltas/player/s (byte budget), lost deltas 0.08 % repaired by acks |
| lockstep 4 x 8 | 32/32 joined, tick mean 0.23 ms, desyncs 0 |

All limits at defaults (`[limits]`): these runs are the regression bar for "limits never cut legitimate
players"; a 128-player join burst from one IP must stay at failed=0.

## Capacity per core (node pinned to 2 cores, bots on the other 6)

`scripts/capacity.sh` runs one load step after another against a node pinned with `taskset -c 0,1`
and reports the node's busy cores (from `/proc/<pid>/stat`), RSS and tick stats per step. Per-IP
limits were raised for the run (`NET__LIMITS__HTTP_RPS_PER_IP`, `WS_CONNECTS_PER_MIN_PER_IP`,
`MAX_SESSIONS_PER_IP`): with the defaults a bot swarm from **one** IP is cut at ~270 players by
`http_rps_per_ip = 200` / `ws_connects_per_min_per_ip = 600` (HTTP 429 on the join burst) — that
is the brute-force guard doing its job, real players arrive from many addresses. 30 s per step,
64-byte events, QUIC data path, 8 players per room.

| mode | rooms × players | node cores busy | RSS | delivery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| relay @ 20 ev/s/player | 40 × 8 (320) | 0.37 | 60 MB | loss 0.1 %, p50 1.7 ms, p99 3.5 ms |
| relay | 80 × 8 (640) | 0.70 | 84 MB | loss 0.4 %, p99 3.7 ms |
| relay | 160 × 8 (1280, ≈180 k deliveries/s) | 1.19 | 136 MB | loss 1.0 %, p99 4.6 ms |
| relay | 320 × 8 (2560) | 1.73 | 229 MB | **saturated**: loss 20 %, p99 10.5 ms |
| relay | 20 × 32 (640, ≈400 k deliveries/s) | 1.58 | 143 MB | loss 2.0 %, p99 6.0 ms |
| sync @ 60 Hz, 20 inputs/s | 40 × 8 (320) | 0.58 | 74 MB | 75.5 deltas/player/s, 0 client gaps |
| sync | 80 × 8 (640) | 1.00 | 98 MB | 74.2 deltas/player/s, lost deltas 0.13 % (acked, repaired) |
| sync | 160 × 8 (1280) | 1.70 | 156 MB | 70.3 deltas/player/s, lost 0.24 %, tick p99 0.2 ms, 0 overruns |
| lockstep @ 60 Hz | 40 × 8 (320) | 0.32 | 121 MB | 0 failed joins, 75.5 frames/player/s |
| lockstep | 80 × 8 (640) | 0.57 | 172 MB | 74.1 frames/player/s |
| lockstep | 160 × 8 (1280) | 1.00 | 259 MB | 71.9 frames/player/s, 0 overruns |

Rule of thumb from this machine (release build, no TLS termination in front): one core carries
≈ 1 000 relay players at 20 ev/s in 8-player rooms (fan-out bound: ≈ 150 k deliveries/s/core),
≈ 750 sync players at 60 Hz, or ≈ 1 250 lockstep players at 60 Hz; RSS ≈ 70–200 KB per player.
Memory, not CPU, is what grows with lockstep (journals + checkpoints per room).

## Soak (1 h, release build, two nodes, bots churning every 5 min)

`scripts/soak-test.sh` runs relay (2 rooms × 8 players @ 20 ev/s, WS tunnel) and sync (1 room × 8 @ 20 Hz)
bots against node B in 300 s batches for an hour — rooms are created, filled, emptied and closed
twelve times — while sampling both nodes' live stats every minute (`/v1/operator/nodes/:id/stats`).

| Node | RSS first / last / max | sync tick p99 max | tick overruns |
|---|---|---|---|
| B (hosting 3 rooms, 24 players) | 20 / 22 / 22 MB | 0.20 ms | 0 |
| A (idle peer: heartbeats, lobby, alert leader) | 13 / 17 / 17 MB | — | 0 |

RSS on both nodes plateaus within the first 30 minutes and stays flat through the remaining room/player
churn: no growth per room lifecycle. Rerun after changes to the room, checkpoint or metering paths;
a steadily climbing RSS across batches is the regression signal.


## Soak 2 — relay + sync + lockstep with forced desyncs (1 h, release, two nodes)

`WEB_KEY=<project key> DURATION=3600 ./scripts/soak-test.sh`: every 5-minute batch runs 2 relay rooms × 8
players (WS tunnel), 1 sync room × 8, 1 lockstep room × 4 at 30 Hz with a late joiner (catch-up from
checkpoint + journal), plus the web `lockstep-live` test whose third client lies about its hash, so the
node collects two desync dumps per batch (stored in Redis for 24 h).

| node | samples | RSS start → end (max) MB | tick p99 max | overruns | rooms / players max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| host (725007) | 61 | 20 → 26 (28) | 0.2 ms | 0 | 7 / 31 |
| idle (087cc9) | 61 | 14 → 18 (18) | 0.2 ms | 0 | 1 / 0 |

Host RSS climbs with the first batches (room churn, dump storage) and stays flat afterwards; no
overruns; desync dumps for every batch were listed and downloadable through `/v1/rooms/:id/desyncs`.

- `NET_HTTP=… NET_API_KEY=… node --test sdk/web/test/referee-live.test.mjs` — lockstep referee: a lying client is flagged by the node's own hash, the node state is stored as desync dump actor 0, room detail reports `referee: true` (upload `crates/net-game/examples/arena.wat` as module `arena` with an admin key first).
- `g++ -std=c++17 sdk/cpp/sync_test.cpp -Isdk/cpp -Ltarget/release -laurix_net -lpthread -ldl -lm -o sync_test && NET_HTTP=… NET_API_KEY=… ./sync_test` — C ABI sync world: two C++ clients in an owner-authoritative sync room, 90 writes of A's Transform replicate to B (85 updates, 87 server ticks, 0 gaps, last position within quantization), A sees exactly one own avatar, render tick lags the server.
- `NET_HTTP=<node A> NET_HTTP_B=<node B> NET_API_KEY=… node --test sdk/web/test/presence-live.test.mjs` — `find_friends` across two nodes (friend in a room on B with room/node, friend only connected on B → online without room, stranger → offline, duplicates collapsed, second request within a second → `lookup_rate`), `stats` with the `ranked` lobby counted, and the idle friend going offline after disconnect.

## Soak 3 — sim referee in lockstep rooms (1 h, release, two nodes)

`WEB_KEY=<key of the project that owns module physics-arena> DURATION=3600 LOCKSTEP_PROPS='{"schema":"…","logic":"physics-arena","position":"Transform.0"}' ./scripts/soak-test.sh`:
the soak 2 pools plus, per 5-minute batch, a second lockstep room (4 bots, late joiner) whose room logic is
the `net-sim-guest` module — the node runs the fixed-point physics itself over confirmed inputs
(`referee: true`) — and the web `referee-live` test (a client lying about its hash every 10 ticks).

**Run 1 (glibc malloc, before the fix) found a real problem**: the host node's RSS stepped up on every
batch, 14 → 189 MB after the first and 264 MB after an hour (p99 tick 0.5 ms, 9 rooms / 34 players max),
while the idle node stayed flat. heaptrack on a node fed six lying-client rounds showed 40 MB peak heap and
140 KB leaked: the memory was freed, glibc just kept its per-thread arenas at their high-water mark. The
bursts came from two places — every desync of the liar made the node build and send a full catch-up
(checkpoint + journal tail), and the first instantiation of a module ran Cranelift on all cores. Fixes:
catch-up only up to `UNTRUSTED_AFTER` strikes, the node binary uses mimalloc, modules compile on one
thread. Reproduce the churn with `sdk/web/test/referee-churn.mjs` (`LIE=1`): before, +3…20 MB per round
and never released; after, a fresh node goes 30 → 100 MB on the first referee room (compile) and then
oscillates 68–76 MB across six lying rounds.

**Run 2 (fixed build, nodes restarted):**

| node | samples | RSS start → end (max) MB | tick p99 max | overruns | rooms / players max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| host (d2eb03) | 62 | 31 → 113 (124) | 0.5 ms | 0 | 9 / 37 |
| idle (f2bb50) | 62 | 31 → 44 (46) | — | 0 | 0 / 0 |

Host RSS is no longer a staircase: 31 MB at start (mimalloc baseline is ~15 MB above glibc), 84–88 MB
through the first four batches, one burst to 118 MB in batch five that mimalloc gave back to 100 MB within
four minutes, and 100–113 MB for the rest of the hour (124 MB peak during the last batch's late join). The
node flagged 276 desyncs from the lying clients (`net_lockstep_desyncs_total`), every referee room reported
`referee: true` and stored its own state as dump actor 0, no tick overruns.

Memory probe before the run (fresh release node, `aurix-net-loadtest --mode lockstep --props-json … --rooms 4
--players 4` repeated 15×, 60 referee rooms created and reaped, no desyncs): RSS 14 MB → 54 MB after the
first instantiation → 64 MB after 60 rooms, flat for the last five rounds and unchanged after all rooms were
reaped; 12 plain lockstep rooms afterwards added 0 MB — the referee rooms themselves do not leak.

## Soak 4 — production image on the compose stack (10 min, distroless, read-only rootfs)

Same pools as soak 3 (`BATCH=120 DURATION=600`, module `physics-arena` uploaded to the stack with
`PUT /v1/modules/physics-arena`) against `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` as shipped: two nodes from the
distroless image (uid 65532, `read_only`, `tmpfs /tmp`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, `no-new-privileges`, nofile
65536), Postgres and Redis on the internal network, console behind Caddy. Point of the run: the hardened
container must not change anything — no writes to the rootfs, no capability the node silently needs, the
built-in `--healthcheck` must keep the container healthy under load.

| node | samples | RSS start → end (max) MB | tick p99 max | overruns | rooms / players max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| host (node-b) | 22 | 29 → 118 (173) | 0.5 ms | 0 | 15 / 37 |
| idle (node-a) | 22 | 31 → 35 (35) | — | 0 | 0 / 0 |

Host RSS: 173 MB on the first sample (first instantiation of the module + the first batch of all pools
starting at once), then 82–93 MB for eight minutes and 101 → 118 MB in the last batch's late join — the
same shape as soak 3 run 2 on bare metal, so mimalloc behaves identically in the container. 207 desyncs
flagged (`net_lockstep_desyncs_total`), Docker health `healthy` throughout, 0 restarts, no OOM, no error
log lines. One stand-specific finding: `GET /v1/operator/nodes/:id/stats` is proxied to the other node via
its `server.public_host`, so with the compose placeholders (`node-b.net.example.com`) it returns 500 until
`PUBLIC_HOST` resolves inside the cluster — documented in deployment.md.

## Multi-host — two machines, shared Postgres/Redis

Setup: node A on a separate 8-vCPU Debian 13 box (Postgres 16 + Redis 7 in Docker next to it),
node B on an Ubuntu 22.04 machine in another network, both pointed at A's Postgres/Redis
(`server.public_host` set to a hostname the *other* machine resolves, `heartbeat_secs=3`).
The remote firewall admitted TCP only, so the data path ran over the WebSocket tunnel
(`transport.ws_tunnel=true`, clients with `--tunnel`); the QUIC/WebTransport data planes were
not exercised across hosts (needs UDP 7000/7443 open end to end).

| check | result |
|---|---|
| registry | both nodes list each other with their own `public_host`, region, heartbeat (`GET /v1/operator/nodes` from either side) |
| placement | rooms created through A land on A (least-loaded node of the *requester's* region, ties keep the room local); a node in another region never receives them unless the client asks for that region |
| relay across the WAN | 6 rooms × 2 bots via A: 2900 events, 0.17 % loss (last tick cut by the run end), p50 180 ms = tunnel RTT |
| drain (SIGTERM on A) | 4 rooms checkpointed to Redis and marked `orphaned` in 4 ms; clients get `left{reason:"rehost"}` |
| matchmaking across hosts | two tickets filed through different nodes (`aurix-net match` via A and via B) matched into the same room within 2 s (Redis-backed queue, one leader) |
| adoption on B | rejoin by name through B adopts the orphaned rows (`adopted orphaned room … restored="none"` for relay); both bots of a pair end up in the **same** room on B, events flow again (p50 1.4 ms locally) |

Bug found and fixed by this run — **adoption race split a room in two.** Two players rejoining
the same orphaned room concurrently through one node: the first `UPDATE rooms SET node_id = me`
succeeded, then spent a few hundred milliseconds (checkpoint read, project lookup, room build —
long on a WAN Redis) before the room was hosted. The second player's lookup saw a row pointing
at this node with no hosted room; the only such case known so far was "creation in progress or a
crash leftover", decided by `created_at < 10 s`. An adopted room is older than that, so the row
was closed and a *new* room with the same name was created: each player sat alone in their own
`lt-4-0`, 100 % of their events had no receiver, and the DB row of the room actually hosted was
marked closed. The node now keeps an in-memory set of rooms it is adopting; a concurrent lookup
answers `room_pending` and the join/join_or_create paths retry for up to 2 s (was 300 ms, join
had no retry at all). Re-run: 2 rooms × 2 bots rehosted A → B, one room per name, 4/4 joined,
events delivered from the moment the second player arrived.

Still needing real infrastructure: UDP data planes across hosts, more than two regions, and
load beyond one node per machine (the capacity table above is single-host).

## Robustness of attacker-facing decoders (`tests/garbage.rs` in each crate)

Every decoder that takes bytes from a peer is fed 20 000 random/mutated inputs per test (a seeded
xorshift, no extra dependencies, runs in `cargo test`): relay `EventFrame::decode`, `Schema::parse`,
`ComponentValue::decode_full/decode_delta`, `Replicator::apply`, `LockstepRoom::handle` and
`SyncRoom::handle` (all frame kinds, player and spectator), `Filter::parse`, the lockstep client
`receive`, transport `Header::decode` / `Reassembler::accept` / `Link::receive` and ticket `verify`.
The first run found a real one: a delta or checkpoint naming entity index `u32::MAX` made
`Frame::ensure_entity` resize the slot table to 170 GB (abort) — and `Frame::restore` trusted the
slot count of a client-uploaded checkpoint/dump the same way. Both now reject anything beyond
`FrameConfig::max_entities` (4096). `cargo audit` is clean (477 crates).

## CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

Two more workflows live next to it: `release.yml` (tag-driven: version/CHANGELOG check, server
bundles for linux x86_64/aarch64, SDK archives, SBOM, multi-arch GHCR images, GitHub Release with
SHA-256 sums) and `soak.yml` (nightly 10-minute two-node soak on a runner — relay + sync +
lockstep bots, RSS/overrun verdict, CSV attached). First run on a GitHub-hosted runner (2 vCPU,
5 min, batch every 2 min): node RSS 40 → 49 MB and 41 → 45 MB, tick p99 ≤ 0.2 ms, 0 overruns.
